What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
,**Short answer – don’t merge everything into one tileset unless you have a very special offline-only use-case.**
For virtually every web-map the recommended pattern is:
1. **Use a hosted (or self-hosted) vector-tile basemap** that already contains roads, water, land-use, place-names, etc.
2. **Add your delivery-zone polygons as a separate source** (GeoJSON for a few thousand zones, or your own vector-tile source if you cross the GeoJSON thresholds).

MapLibre will request both sources in parallel, and there is no per-source rendering penalty. This keeps the basemap up-to-date, respects OSM licensing, and lets you change the style of the basemap without rebuilding your data.
## Why a “single source” isn’t a performance win

column3: What a single combined tileset would do
column4: What the two-source pattern does

column3: Same total tile bytes (you still have to download the basemap tiles plus your polygons).
column4: Same total bytes, but tiles are fetched concurrently from independent URLs.

column3: Every time you edit a delivery-zone you must rebuild the whole OSM-plus-your-data tileset (potentially millions of tiles).
column4: You only rebuild the small delivery-zone tileset (or even just update a GeoJSON file).

column3: You lose the ability to swap to a newer OSM style or a different provider without re-generating the whole combined set.
column4: You can point the style at a newer basemap URL instantly; your overlay stays unchanged.

column3: You become a redistributor of OSM data and must embed OSM attribution in every tile you serve.
column4: You simply consume the basemap provider’s attribution (often already handled by the style) and add your own attribution separately.

column3: You need a full tile-generation pipeline (extract → merge → tile → host).
column4: You only need a pipeline for your own data (or none at all if you stay with GeoJSON).

column1: Because MapLibre already handles multiple sources efficiently, “one source” does **not** reduce rendering cost or latency. It only adds operational overhead.
## When a single combined tileset *might* be justified

A single tileset makes sense only for **offline, air-gapped, or single-file deployments** where the map must work without any network connection (e.g., a field-device app shipped on a USB stick). In that narrow scenario you can bake everything into one vector-tile archive (MBTiles, PMTiles, etc.).
Below is a **high-level pipeline** you can follow. I’m naming the tools you would use, but I’m not providing a line-by-line script—just the logical steps so you can adapt them to your environment.
## High-level pipeline to merge OSM data with your delivery-zone polygons

* **OpenStreetMap data** is © OpenStreetMap contributors, under the ODbL. When you redistribute OSM tiles you must:
* Include the OSM attribution in the map UI (MapLibre style `metadata.attribution` or a custom HTML overlay).
* Provide a link to the OSM license.

* If you modify OSM data (e.g., merge with your polygons), you must also make the derived data available under the same ODbL terms, unless you have a separate licensing arrangement with the OSM contributors (rare).

Because the two-source pattern keeps the basemap as a *consumed* service, you can rely on the basemap provider (e.g., OpenMapTiles, MapTiler, or a public OSM tile service) to handle the OSM attribution for you. ,Below is a complete, step-by-step recipe for turning a single scanned JPG (or PNG, TIFF, etc.) into a **georeferenced image overlay** that you can turn on/off or fade in/out on a MapLibre GL JS map.

column1: MapLibre expects the four corners **in clockwise order** starting with the **top-left** (north-west) corner:
If you only have the four lat/lon pairs, just put them in that order.
*(If you have them in a different order, re-order them before you paste them into the source definition.)*
// Assuming you already have a MapLibre map instance called `map`
url: '/assets/1920s-city.jpg',   // <-- change to your actual URL
// The four corner coordinates (lon, lat) in clockwise order
* **CORS** – If the image lives on a different domain, that server must send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` (or your origin). Otherwise the image will fail to load and you’ll see a console error.

* **Large images** – If the JPG is > 5 MB you’ll see a noticeable download time. For very large historic maps you can pre-tile them (see the “When to use tiles” section below) but for a single city-scale sheet an `image` source is usually fine.
## 3. Add a raster layer that uses the source
